title: Photons in the Schwarzschild geometry
one_line_summary: Runs light through the same conserved-quantity machinery already used for planets: the null condition becomes an effective-energy equation with a photon potential W_eff = (1 - 2M/r)/r^2 that does not care about angular momentum, whose single peak at r = 3M marks the unstable photon sphere and the capture threshold b = sqrt(27) M; the orbit equation u'' + u = 3u^2, perturbed about a straight line, gives the 4M/b deflection (quoted as about 1.8 arcsec for a ray grazing the Sun, 1.75 with precise solar values; the 1919 eclipse test); a point mass is shown to be an imperfect lens with Einstein rings; and photon momenta transferred to a static observer's frame give a critical emission angle that turns, by time reversal, into a dark patch on the sky.
role_in_book: Third of the four Schwarzschild chapters (21 metric, 22 constants of motion and redshift, 23 massive orbits and perihelion precession). It reuses Chapter 22's E-tilde and L-tilde and Chapter 23's effective-potential and u-substitution recipes almost line for line, now for null geodesics, so that the second classical solar-system test (light bending) can be computed and compared with Soldner's Newtonian value. Its closing section, on what a static observer sees, supplies the critical angle and the photon sphere that Chapter 25 (black holes, especially 25.4 on looking around near a hole and the Event Horizon Telescope image) builds on, and Exercise 24.4 on the affine parameter along a light ray is explicitly reused in Exercise 26.4. The chapter-end table unifies the coordinate-time equations for massive and massless motion as a reference for the black-hole chapters.

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild line element, geometrized units and the meaning of r as an areal coordinate
Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass read off from the metric's t- and phi-independence
Relativistic effective potential V_eff for massive particles, its maximum as an unstable circular orbit, and the u = M/r orbit equation
Newtonian effective potentials and the Binet-type orbit equation (eqn 20.33)
Null geodesics, the affine parameter and the null tangent condition
Orthonormal frames and vielbein components for a static observer
Photon four-momentum p = E u in flat spacetime
Weak-field link between g_00 and the Newtonian potential
Robertson-Walker line element and the chi radial coordinate (Exercise 24.4 only)
Linear second-order ODEs with constant coefficients and a trigonometric forcing term; small-angle and first-order expansions
Refractive index, Fermat's principle of least time, and thin-lens ray diagrams
Solar eclipses, arc seconds, the solar radius and apparent stellar positions

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a light ray that is a null geodesic of spacetime can still trace a bent path in space, using the position-dependent coordinate speed of light and a Fermat-principle picture.
Reader can derive the photon effective-energy equation 1/b^2 = (dr/dlambda)^2/L^2 + W_eff from the Schwarzschild null condition and the conserved E-tilde and L-tilde.
Reader can show that b = L-tilde/E-tilde equals the geometric impact parameter of a ray that starts at infinity.

Reader can sketch W_eff(r), locate its maximum at r = 3M with value 1/(27M^2), and classify incoming rays as scattered (b > sqrt(27) M), captured (b < sqrt(27) M) or marginally orbiting on the unstable photon sphere.
Reader can convert the null condition into the orbit equation (du/dphi)^2 = M^2/b^2 - u^2 + 2u^3 and u'' + u = 3u^2, and identify 3u^2 as the relativistic correction to straight-line motion.
Reader can perturb about the straight-line solution u0 = (M/b) sin phi, solve for u1, and extract the total deflection 4M/b from the asymptotic directions where u = 0.

Reader can evaluate 4GM/(c^2 b) for a ray grazing the Sun (about 1.75 arcsec), state that it is twice the Newtonian corpuscular value, and summarize the 1919 eclipse test and later radio confirmations with their caveats.
Reader can show that a point mass focuses rays at a distance D = b^2/4M that grows with b, explain why this means no single focus, and describe when an Einstein ring forms.
Reader can derive the small-angle point-lens equation theta_i = theta_s + theta_E^2/theta_i from a ray diagram and define the Einstein angle.
Reader can build photon four-momentum components in Schwarzschild coordinates as the massless limit of m dx/dtau at fixed energy at infinity, and express them in terms of epsilon and b.
Reader can use static-observer vielbeins to get sin psi = (b/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} and the critical angle sin psi_c = (sqrt(27) M/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}, choosing the correct branch above and below r = 3M.
Reader can use time-reversal symmetry of the static geometry to argue that directions inside the capture cone look black to a static observer, anticipating the black-hole shadow.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, reuse-driven chapter. Instead of solving the null geodesic equation, the authors recycle the Chapter 22-23 template (conserved quantities plus a normalization condition gives an energy equation, then an orbit equation in u) and rename the pieces for light, so almost every new result is a small modification of something the reader has just done for planets. Physics is kept in front: an optics heuristic opens the chapter, the potential plot is read qualitatively before any orbit is solved, solar numbers and the eclipse story follow the perturbative deflection formula immediately, and the lens analogy is both used and deliberately broken. The final section changes the question from 'where does the ray go' to 'what does an observer see', using vielbeins from Chapter 10 and a time-reversal argument to set up the black-hole chapter. Most calculations sit in shaded Example boxes; the chapter ends with a two-part reference table.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: in Newtonian gravity as developed so far light ignores gravity, yet Soldner's corpuscular reasoning already predicted a small bending near the Sun; what does GR say?
Heuristic (Example 24.1): in a static metric the coordinate speed of light varies with position, so gravity acts like a graded refractive index and a Fermat least-time principle bends spatial rays.
Model: photons follow null geodesics labelled by an affine parameter; the conserved E-tilde and L-tilde from Chapter 22 still apply because they came from symmetry, not from proper time.
Formalism: rewrite the null condition as an effective-energy equation with 1/b^2 as the energy and W_eff(r) as a potential independent of L-tilde.
Interpretation: identify b as the impact parameter (Example 24.2) and read Fig. 24.2 for scattering, capture and the unstable photon sphere at r = 3M.
Orbit equation (Example 24.3): switch to u = M/r and differentiate to get u'' + u = 3u^2, contrasting with Newtonian straight lines u'' + u = 0.

Check against experiment (Examples 24.4-24.5): perturb around a straight line, find a 4M/b deflection, plug in solar numbers, compare with Soldner, recount Eddington 1919 with caveats and later radio confirmation.
Extension and critique (Example 24.6): treat the mass as a lens, show the focal distance depends on b so there is no focus, and introduce the Einstein ring (exercises develop the lens equation).
New question (Section 24.2): what does an observer at radius r see? Build photon momentum as the m -> 0 limit at fixed energy at infinity (Example 24.7).
Measurement: convert to the static observer's orthonormal frame with vielbeins to get the emission angle psi, then the critical angle psi_c and its shrinking escape cone as r -> 2M.

Hand-off: time-reversal symmetry turns captured emission directions into a black region of the observer's sky, setting up black holes; the summary table collects massive and photon equations side by side.
signature_moves: Dictionary-style reuse of the massive-particle energy equation: 1/b^2 plays total energy, (dr/dlambda)^2/L^2 plays kinetic energy, W_eff plays the potential.
Opening with an optics picture (coordinate light speed as a refractive index, Fermat's principle) before any geodesic calculation, while flagging it only as partial justification.
Isolating the relativistic physics in a single extra term (3u^2) by writing the photon orbit equation next to its Newtonian straight-line limit.
Perturbing about the flat-space straight line and reading the deflection off the two asymptotic angles where 1/r vanishes, instead of integrating an elliptic integral.
Immediate numbers and history after the formula: solar grazing ray, factor of two over Soldner, Eddington's eclipse, and a note that his systematics were later questioned.
Stress-testing an analogy: a mass deflects like a lens but its focal distance scales as b^2, so the analogy fails and rings rather than points appear.
Defining photon momentum as a limit of the massive formula with energy at infinity held fixed, so the undefined dtau for light never appears.
Translating coordinate components into what a static observer measures via vielbeins, yielding an angle whose form r sin(psi) = b(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} echoes flat-space geometry.
Using time reversal of a static spacetime to convert an emission statement (photons that fall in) into an observation statement (a black region of sky).
Ending with a side-by-side table of massive and massless equations of motion in the equatorial plane.

sections.title: Chapter opening: can gravity bend light?
sections.summary: Notes that in the Newtonian picture used so far light moves in straight lines, then mentions Soldner's early corpuscular estimate of about 0.8 arcsec for starlight skimming the Sun (with margin credit to Cavendish, Michell and Newton). Example 24.1 gives a first reason light should bend in GR: for a static diagonal metric the null condition makes the light speed measured in coordinate time depend on g_00, which behaves like a refractive index, and the spatial path obeys a Fermat least-time principle built from g_ij/(-g_00).
concepts: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime
key_moves: Set ds^2 = 0 for a static diagonal metric and solve for the coordinate speed c'^2 = -c^2 g_00 (eqn 24.2).
Link g_00 to the Newtonian potential (margin note 3) so c' visibly depends on position.
Separate the ideas 'null geodesic in spacetime' and 'geodesic in space': the former need not be the latter.
State without proof that spatial rays extremize the integral of sqrt(g_ij dx^i dx^j/(-g_00)) (eqn 24.3) as partial justification for bending.

sections.title: Photon trajectories: effective energy, impact parameter and the photon potential
sections.summary: Photons have no proper time, so world lines are labelled with an affine parameter and obey the null condition. Writing that condition in Schwarzschild spacetime with the conserved E-tilde and L-tilde and rescaling gives an effective-energy equation whose energy is 1/b^2 and whose potential W_eff = (1 - 2M/r)/r^2 does not involve L-tilde. Example 24.2 shows b = L/E is the impact parameter of an incoming ray. The potential has one maximum, 1/(27M^2) at r = 3M, and no minimum: rays with b above sqrt(27) M bounce off the hill and are deflected, rays below it plunge to r = 0, and exactly at the peak there are circular but unstable orbits on the photon sphere; no stable light orbits exist.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics
key_moves: Replace proper time by an affine parameter and impose u.u = 0 (eqn 24.4).
Substitute u^t = E/(1 - 2M/r) and u^phi = L/r^2 into the null condition (eqn 24.5).
Multiply by (1 - 2M/r) and divide by L^2 to reach 1/b^2 = (dr/dlambda)^2/L^2 + W_eff with W_eff = (1 - 2M/r)/r^2 (eqns 24.6-24.7).
Evaluate L/E far from the mass for a straight ray at offset d, using phi ~ d/r and dr/dt ~ -1, to show b = d (eqns 24.8-24.9).
Set dW_eff/dr = 0 to get r0 = 3M and W_eff(r0) = 1/(27M^2); compare 1/b^2 with this peak to sort rays into scattered, captured and orbiting.
Note that the absence of a minimum rules out stable circular photon orbits.

sections.title: Photon trajectories (continued): the orbit equation
sections.summary: Example 24.3 derives the shape equation for equatorial rays. Dividing the null condition by (u^phi)^2 turns it into an equation for dr/dphi; the time term is rewritten with lowered components so that 1/b^2 appears; substituting u = M/r gives (du/dphi)^2 = M^2/b^2 - u^2 + 2u^3, and differentiating gives u'' + u = 3u^2. Setting the particle mass to zero in the Newtonian orbit equation of Chapter 20 gives u'' + u = 0 (straight lines), so the 3u^2 term carries all of the relativistic bending.
key_moves: Write dr/dphi = u^r/u^phi (eqn 24.10) and divide the null condition by (u^phi)^2 (eqns 24.11-24.12).
Use raised and lowered components (margin note 5) to replace the time ratio by -(1 - 2M/r)^{-1} r^4/b^2.
Substitute u = M/r to reach the first integral (eqn 24.15) and differentiate to reach eqn 24.16.
Compare with the massless limit of the Newtonian orbit equation (eqn 20.33) to isolate the correction term.

sections.title: Photon trajectories (continued): deflection of starlight by the Sun
sections.summary: Light bending is introduced as the second classical solar-system test. Example 24.4 treats M/b as small, starts from the straight line u0 = (M/b) sin phi, and solves the forced equation for the first correction u1, obtaining a trajectory whose two zeros of u sit slightly beyond phi = 0 and phi = pi; the extra 2M/b at each end adds to a total deflection of 4M/b. Example 24.5 restores G and c for a ray grazing the Sun to get about 8.6e-6 rad, roughly 1.8 arcsec and about twice Soldner's figure, then recounts Eddington's 1919 eclipse measurement, its role in making Einstein famous, later doubts about its systematic errors, and modern radio-source measurements that agree well with GR. A rubber-sheet cartoon (Fig. 24.4) shows the apparent shift of a star.
concepts: classical solar-system tests of general relativity
key_moves: Choose the zeroth-order straight-line solution u0 = (M/b) sin phi of the Newtonian equation (eqn 24.17).
Insert u = u0 + u1 and keep only 3u0^2 on the right; use sin^2 = (1 - cos 2phi)/2 (eqns 24.18-24.19).
Solve with a constant plus a cos 2phi particular solution, u1 = (1/2)(M/b)^2 (3 + cos 2phi) (eqns 24.20-24.21).
Find the asymptotes from u = 0, which gives phi ~ -2M/b and phi ~ pi + 2M/b, so the ray turns through 4M/b in total.
Restore constants: Delta phi = 4GM/(c^2 b) for b = R_sun gives about 1.8 arcsec (eqn 24.23).

sections.title: Photon trajectories (continued): gravitational lensing and the Einstein ring
sections.summary: Because masses deflect light they act somewhat like lenses, but Example 24.6 shows the analogy is imperfect: a parallel ray at distance b crosses the axis a distance D = b/theta = b^2/4M behind the mass, so outer rays focus farther away and there is no single focal point. When source, lens and observer are collinear, the symmetric bending produces a ring image (the Einstein ring, Fig. 24.5b); the exercises build the small-angle lens equation and the Einstein angle.
key_moves: Use the small-angle relation D = b/theta with theta = 4M/b to get D = b^2/4M (eqn 24.24).
Contrast with a glass lens, for which D would be the same for all b.
Invoke axial symmetry for an aligned source to turn two images into a ring.

sections.title: Looking around: photon momentum in Schwarzschild coordinates
sections.summary: To ask what an observer sees, the chapter needs photon four-momentum. Example 24.7 starts from a massive particle, writes p = m (dx/dt) u^t, trades u^t for E-tilde/(1 - 2M/r), and names m E-tilde the energy at infinity epsilon; the resulting expression survives the limit m -> 0 and so defines photon momentum, at the cost of being tied to coordinate time. Using b = r^2 (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} dphi/dt and the null condition divided by dt^2 fixes dr/dt, giving p^t = epsilon/(1 - 2M/r), p^r = +/- epsilon [1 - (b^2/r^2)(1 - 2M/r)]^{1/2}, p^theta = 0 and p^phi = epsilon b/r^2.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics
key_moves: Recall the flat-spacetime relation p^mu = E u^mu for photons.
Write p^mu = m (dx^mu/dt)(dt/dtau) and replace dt/dtau using E-tilde (eqns 24.25-24.27).
Hold epsilon = m E-tilde fixed and let m -> 0 (eqn 24.28), giving coordinate components (eqn 24.29).
Divide the null condition by dt^2 and use b to solve for dr/dt (eqns 24.30-24.31), then assemble eqn 24.32.

sections.title: Looking around (continued): critical emission angle and the dark part of the sky
sections.summary: A static emitter at radius r sends photons at angle psi measured in its own orthonormal frame from the outward radial direction (Fig. 24.6). The sine of psi is the ratio of sideways to time components of momentum in that frame; converting with the vielbeins (e_t)^t-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} and (e_phi)^phi-hat = r gives sin psi = (b/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}. Setting b = sqrt(27) M defines a critical angle beyond which rays have 1/b^2 above the peak of W_eff (Fig. 24.7) and fall in; the escaping fraction shrinks as r falls and vanishes at r = 2M. Because the static geometry is unchanged under time reversal, the same cones describe reception: directions whose backward rays would come from the hole bring no light, so that part of the observer's sky is black, the theme of the next chapter.
concepts: time-reversal symmetry of a static spacetime
key_moves: Define sin psi = u^phi-hat/u^t-hat = p^phi-hat/p^t-hat in the emitter's local frame (eqn 24.33).
Convert coordinate components with vielbeins (eqn 24.34, margin note 9) and insert eqn 24.32 to get eqn 24.35.
Impose the capture threshold b = sqrt(27) M to get sin psi_c = (sqrt(27) M/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}.
Track how the capture cone widens as r decreases, until everything is captured at r = 2M.
Reverse the film: emission cones become viewing cones, and the captured directions appear black.

sections.title: Chapter summary and equations-of-motion table
sections.summary: Three bullet points (photons are deflected; an effective-energy equation gives the deflection; light bending is a classical test that GR passes) followed by a reference table of equatorial motion in Schwarzschild spacetime: for massive particles the constants E-tilde and L-tilde and expressions for dr/dtau, dr/dt and dphi/dt; for photons the constant b and expressions for dr/dt and dphi/dt.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics
key_moves: Collect coordinate-time velocities so massive and massless motion can be compared term by term.
(Our reading aid, not done in the book) Check that the photon rows follow from the massive rows when E-tilde and L-tilde grow without bound at fixed ratio b.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Four problems: verify the photon energy equation and potential; verify the perturbative deflection trajectory; derive the small-angle point-lens equation from a ray diagram and the Einstein ring size for an aligned source at infinity; and, for a radial light ray in a Robertson-Walker universe, reduce the metric to t and chi, show the chi component of the tangent scales as 1/a^2, and integrate for the affine parameter, with a pointer to Exercise 26.4.
concepts: radial light rays in Robertson-Walker spacetime
key_moves: Practise the algebra behind eqns 24.6-24.7 and 24.19-24.21.
Build the lens equation by equating transverse offsets in the source plane.
Use a cyclic coordinate in a cosmological metric to find a conserved tangent component and hence the affine parameter.

concepts.name: null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic whose tangent vector has zero length at every point, g_{mu nu} (dx^mu/dlambda)(dx^nu/dlambda) = 0 with lambda affine; freely propagating light follows such curves.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the key physical input for photons right after noting that proper time cannot label a light ray; combined with the Schwarzschild metric it replaces the u.u = -1 normalization used for planets.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a curve in which the geodesic equation takes its standard form; it is unique up to lambda -> a lambda + b and is needed for null curves, where proper time does not advance.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a stand-in for proper time that ticks off equal steps along a photon world line; Exercise 24.4 later shows how to compute it along a cosmological light ray.
concepts.notes: For photons the normalization of lambda is arbitrary, so E-tilde and L-tilde individually have no absolute meaning; only b = L/E is physical.

concepts.name: coordinate speed of light
concepts.definition: The rate at which a light signal covers coordinate distance per unit coordinate time. In a static diagonal metric the null condition gives g_ij v^i v^j = -c^2 g_00, so it varies with position even though any local observer measures c.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.1 sets ds^2 = 0 for a static diagonal metric and reads off c'; a margin note ties g_00 to the Newtonian potential so c' visibly changes near a mass.

concepts.name: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime
concepts.definition: In a static spacetime the spatial track of a light ray makes the integral of sqrt(g_ij dx^i dx^j/(-g_00)) stationary; equivalently it is a geodesic of the rescaled 3-metric g_ij/(-g_00), which extremizes coordinate travel time.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without proof in Example 24.1 as partial justification for bending, after pointing out that a null geodesic of spacetime need not be a geodesic of space.

concepts.name: gravitational refractive index
aliases: effective refractive index of a gravitational field
concepts.definition: The ratio of c to the coordinate speed of light, which lets a static gravitational field be modelled as an inhomogeneous optical medium; in isotropic weak-field coordinates n is about 1 - 2 Phi/c^2, larger nearer the mass, so rays bend toward it.
concepts.how_introduced: Suggested in Example 24.1 by the observation that the g_00 factor in the light-speed formula looks like an index of refraction.
prerequisites: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime
concepts.notes: The book loosely calls sqrt(-g_00) the index; with a flat spatial metric the index is 1/sqrt(-g_00), and keeping only g_00 reproduces just half the full GR deflection (the spatial metric supplies the rest).

concepts.name: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics
aliases: constants of the motion for light
concepts.definition: Because the Schwarzschild metric does not depend on t or phi, E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dlambda and L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dlambda (equatorial plane) are constant along any geodesic, null ones included, when lambda is an affine parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: A margin note stresses that these constants came from symmetry arguments in the previous chapters, not from proper time, so they carry over to photons unchanged.

concepts.name: photon effective-energy equation
concepts.definition: The Schwarzschild null condition rewritten as a one-dimensional energy balance 1/b^2 = (1/L^2)(dr/dlambda)^2 + W_eff(r), where 1/b^2 plays total energy and (dr/dlambda)^2/L^2 plays kinetic energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by writing the null condition in terms of E-tilde and L-tilde, multiplying by (1 - 2M/r) and dividing by L^2, explicitly mirroring the energy equation for massive particles in Chapters 22-23.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

concepts.name: photon effective potential
concepts.definition: W_eff(r) = (1/r^2)(1 - 2M/r). It is negative inside r = 2M, zero at 2M, rises to a single maximum 1/(27M^2) at r = 3M and falls off as 1/r^2 at large r; it has no minimum and, unlike V_eff for massive particles, contains no angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the potential term of the photon energy equation and immediately plotted (Fig. 24.2) and compared with the Newtonian and relativistic potentials for massive particles.
concepts.notes: Because the angular momentum has been scaled into 1/b^2, every ray meets the same hill; which rays pass depends only on b.

concepts.name: impact parameter
concepts.definition: The perpendicular distance between a mass and the straight-line asymptote of an incoming ray; for Schwarzschild null geodesics it equals the ratio b = L-tilde/E-tilde, which is independent of how the affine parameter is normalized.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.2 evaluates L/E far from the mass for a ray travelling parallel to the x-axis at height d (Fig. 24.1), using phi ~ d/r and dr/dt ~ -1, and finds b = d; the text adds that b grows with angular momentum and shrinks with energy.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

concepts.name: photon sphere
concepts.definition: The sphere r = 3M on which circular null geodesics exist, for rays with b = sqrt(27) M sitting exactly at the peak of W_eff; since it is a maximum, any perturbation sends light either inward or out to infinity, so these orbits are unstable.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off Fig. 24.2 by analogy with the unstable circular orbit at the maximum of V_eff for massive particles.

concepts.name: critical impact parameter
concepts.definition: The impact parameter b_c = sqrt(27) M = 3 sqrt(3) M (about 5.2 M) at which 1/b^2 equals the peak of W_eff; incoming rays with larger b are deflected and escape, rays with smaller b are captured.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by comparing the photon energy level 1/b^2 with the maximum 1/(27M^2) of W_eff, then reused in Section 24.2 to define the critical emission angle.

concepts.name: photon capture
concepts.definition: A ray moving inward whose 1/b^2 exceeds the maximum of W_eff meets no turning point and continues to smaller r, through r = 2M and on to r = 0 in these coordinates; outside 3M an outward-moving ray escapes whatever its b.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated from the potential plot for incoming rays with small impact parameter, then applied to rays emitted near the mass in Section 24.2 (Figs. 24.6 and 24.7).
concepts.notes: The book describes captured photons as 'destroyed' at r = 0; the horizon at 2M and the nature of r = 0 are postponed to Chapters 25-26.

concepts.name: photon orbit equation
concepts.definition: The equation for the path r(phi) of an equatorial light ray in Schwarzschild spacetime, in u = M/r: (du/dphi)^2 = M^2/b^2 - u^2 + 2u^3, or after differentiation u'' + u = 3u^2; without the right-hand side its solutions are straight lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.3 divides the null condition by (u^phi)^2, rewrites the time term via lowered components so that 1/b^2 appears, substitutes u = M/r, and differentiates; the massless Newtonian limit of eqn 20.33 is shown for contrast.

concepts.name: Binet substitution
concepts.definition: Replacing the radius by its inverse (here the dimensionless u = M/r) and using phi as the independent variable, which turns central-force orbit equations into forced oscillator equations whose Newtonian solutions are straight lines or conics.
concepts.how_introduced: Reused from the massive-orbit chapters; a margin note also gives the straight line in polar form u = 1/r so the zeroth-order solution is recognizable.

concepts.name: perturbation about the straight-line solution
concepts.definition: Writing u = u0 + u1 with u0 = (M/b) sin phi the flat-space straight line, inserting into u'' + u = 3u^2 and keeping only 3u0^2 as the source, so that u1 is a small correction of order (M/b)^2 found by elementary methods.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.4 motivates it by the smallness of M/b for starlight passing the Sun, uses the identity sin^2 phi = (1 - cos 2phi)/2 and a constant plus cos 2phi trial solution.

concepts.name: gravitational light deflection
concepts.definition: The total change in direction of a ray passing a spherical mass with impact parameter b; to first order in M/b it is 4M/b, that is 4GM/(c^2 b), and it does not depend on the photon's energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in Example 24.4 from the two angles where u = 0 on the perturbed trajectory; Example 24.5 evaluates it for a ray grazing the Sun and connects it to the eclipse test.
concepts.notes: Text and Fig. 24.3 use Delta phi inconsistently: in the figure Delta phi is the total angle swept and delta phi the deflection.

concepts.name: Newtonian corpuscular light deflection
concepts.definition: The deflection obtained by treating light as fast particles in Newtonian gravity, 2GM/(c^2 b), half the GR value; for a grazing solar ray it is a bit under 1 arcsec.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the chapter opening (Soldner, about 0.8 arcsec) as a pre-relativistic foil, and recalled when the GR result is found to be roughly twice as large.

concepts.name: classical solar-system tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: The historic trio of perihelion precession of Mercury, the bending of starlight by the Sun, and gravitational redshift (with radar echo delay often added as a fourth).
concepts.how_introduced: Light deflection is labelled the second of these tests, following perihelion precession in Chapter 23.

concepts.name: 1919 eclipse expedition
concepts.definition: Photographic measurement of the positions of stars near the Sun during the total eclipse of May 1919, compared with their night-time positions, to test for the predicted outward shift of about 1.75 arcsec at the limb.
concepts.how_introduced: Recounted in Example 24.5 immediately after the numerical prediction, together with its public impact and later questioning of the error analysis.
concepts.notes: The book cites Earman and Glymour (1980) for the history but gives no measured values.

concepts.name: radio interferometric light-deflection measurements
concepts.definition: Measurements of the apparent angular shifts of compact radio sources such as quasars as their lines of sight pass near the Sun, which avoid the need for an eclipse and reach far higher precision than optical plates.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in one sentence as the modern high-precision confirmation of the GR deflection.

concepts.name: gravitational lensing
concepts.definition: The formation of displaced, magnified, multiple or ring-shaped images of a background source because light from it is deflected by an intervening mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a loose analogy (masses behave somewhat like lenses) that the next example then qualifies.

concepts.name: gravitational lens focal distance
aliases: no single focus of a point-mass lens
concepts.definition: For parallel rays passing a point mass, a ray at impact parameter b crosses the symmetry axis a distance D = b^2/4M behind the mass, so different annuli focus at different distances and the lens has a focal line rather than a focal point.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.6 applies the small-angle relation D = b/theta to theta = 4M/b (Fig. 24.5a) and contrasts the result with an ideal lens.

concepts.name: Einstein ring
concepts.definition: The circular image formed when a point source, a spherically symmetric lens and the observer lie on one line, so that rays deflected by the same angle arrive from every azimuth around the lens.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after Example 24.6 and illustrated as a cone of rays traced back from the observer (Fig. 24.5b); its angular size is left to Exercise 24.3.

concepts.name: Einstein angle
concepts.definition: The characteristic angular scale of a point-mass lens, theta_E = sqrt(4M D_ls/(D_l D_s)) with D_l, D_s and D_ls the observer-lens, observer-source and lens-source distances; it is the ring radius for perfect alignment.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined inside Exercise 24.3 while deriving the lens equation from the ray diagram of Fig. 24.8.

concepts.name: point-mass lens equation
concepts.definition: Small-angle relation between the observed image angle theta_i and the true source angle theta_s for a point-mass lens: theta_i = theta_s + theta_E^2/theta_i, which has two image solutions for theta_s nonzero and a ring for theta_s = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Set as Exercise 24.3: equate transverse distances in the source plane, using the deflection 4M/b with b = theta_i D_l.

concepts.name: photon four-momentum in Schwarzschild spacetime
concepts.definition: Components of a photon's momentum in Schwarzschild coordinates, defined as the massless limit of the massive formula at fixed energy at infinity: p^t = epsilon/(1 - 2M/r), p^r = +/- epsilon [1 - (b^2/r^2)(1 - 2M/r)]^{1/2}, p^theta = 0, p^phi = epsilon b/r^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 24.7 starts from m dx/dtau, trades dt/dtau for E-tilde, names m E-tilde the energy at infinity, lets m -> 0, and then removes dr/dt and dphi/dt using b and the null condition.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics
concepts.notes: The construction ties p to coordinate time t, which the book flags as the price paid.

concepts.name: energy at infinity
concepts.definition: The conserved quantity epsilon = m E-tilde (for a photon, the limit of this product) equal to the energy a static observer far from the mass would measure; locally measured energies differ from it by redshift factors.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in Example 24.7 so that a finite parameter remains when the rest mass is sent to zero.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

concepts.name: static observer orthonormal frame
aliases: vielbein for a static Schwarzschild observer
local frame of a hovering observer
concepts.definition: The orthonormal basis carried by an observer at fixed r, theta, phi, related to coordinate components by (e_t)^t-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}, (e_r)^r-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2}, (e_theta)^theta-hat = r and (e_phi)^phi-hat = r in the equatorial plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in Section 24.2 with a margin list of vielbein components to convert photon momentum into what the emitter measures.

concepts.name: locally measured emission angle
aliases: angle from the radial direction in the static frame
concepts.definition: The angle psi between a photon's direction and the outward radial direction as measured in a static observer's orthonormal frame; sin psi = p^phi-hat/p^t-hat = (b/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined with the construction in Fig. 24.6, whose flat-space geometry r sin psi = b is corrected by the factor (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} once the vielbeins are applied.

concepts.name: critical emission angle
concepts.definition: The value of psi for which the emitted ray has b = sqrt(27) M: sin psi_c = (sqrt(27) M/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}. It separates emission directions that escape from those that are captured; outside 3M the captured cone surrounds the inward direction, inside 3M only a cone around the outward direction escapes, and at r = 2M nothing escapes.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by setting b to its critical value in the emission-angle formula; the text notes the capture region widens as the emitter moves inward (Figs. 24.6-24.7).
concepts.notes: Because sin is not one-to-one on [0, pi], psi_c is obtuse for r > 3M and acute for r < 3M; the book does not spell out the branch choice.

concepts.name: time-reversal symmetry of a static spacetime
concepts.definition: A static metric is unchanged under t -> -t, so every null geodesic run backwards is again a null geodesic; the rules for emitted rays therefore also describe received rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in the last paragraph of Section 24.2 as a film-played-backwards argument turning the capture cone for emission into a region of sky that sends no light.

concepts.name: black-hole shadow
aliases: capture cone seen by an observer
concepts.definition: The patch of an observer's sky, bounded by rays with b = sqrt(27) M, from which no light arrives because tracing those directions backwards leads into the hole rather than to a light source; for a distant observer its angular radius is about sqrt(27) M/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Implied rather than named: the book concludes that directions with psi beyond psi_c are black and defers the consequences to the black-hole chapter.
prerequisites: time-reversal symmetry of a static spacetime
concepts.notes: Strictly it is black only if nothing inside the photon sphere emits; an extended star larger than 3M would fill those directions with its own light.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The static, spherically symmetric vacuum solution ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 in geometrized units.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from Chapter 21; its components are inserted in the null condition and orbit equation.

concepts.name: relativistic effective potential
concepts.definition: The potential V_eff = -M/r + L^2/(2r^2) - M L^2/r^3 in the massive-particle energy equation of Chapter 23, which has a stable minimum and an unstable maximum for large enough L-tilde.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled for contrast: W_eff shares the maximum but not the minimum and has no L dependence.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

concepts.name: radial light rays in Robertson-Walker spacetime
aliases: chi coordinate for radial null rays
concepts.definition: For purely radial motion the Robertson-Walker metric reduces to ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 dchi^2 with dchi = dr/(1 - kr^2)^{1/2}; chi is cyclic, so a^2 u^chi is constant along the ray, giving u^chi = C/a^2 and an explicit integral for the affine parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only as Exercise 24.4, which transplants the conserved-quantity method to cosmology and points ahead to Exercise 26.4.
prerequisites: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: Units in which G and c are set to one, so mass is measured as a length M = GM_phys/c^2; constants are restored when numbers are needed.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout; constants are put back in Example 24.5 and c appears explicitly in Example 24.1.

key_equations.name: Straight line in polar form
key_equations.meaning: A Newtonian photon path y = mx + c written in terms of inverse radius, the form against which relativistic rays are compared.
key_equations.symbols: m slope, c intercept on y axis (not the speed of light), theta polar angle

key_equations.name: Coordinate speed of light in a static metric
key_equations.meaning: Setting ds^2 = 0 for a static diagonal metric shows the coordinate speed of light depends on g_00 and hence on position.
key_equations.symbols: g_00, g_ij metric components; c' coordinate light speed

key_equations.name: Weak-field g_00 (margin note 3, corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Relates the coordinate light speed to the Newtonian potential. The margin prints sqrt(-g_00) ~ 1 + 2 Phi, which mixes the two forms; the square root carries only one Phi.
key_equations.symbols: Phi Newtonian potential in units c = 1

key_equations.name: Fermat's principle for static spacetimes
key_equations.meaning: The spatial projection of a light ray is a geodesic of the optical metric g_ij/(-g_00), i.e. it makes coordinate travel time stationary.
key_equations.symbols: delta variation of the path

key_equations.name: Null condition
key_equations.meaning: Photon tangent vectors have zero length; replaces u.u = -1 used for massive particles.
key_equations.symbols: lambda affine parameter; u tangent vector

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild null condition in conserved quantities
key_equations.meaning: The null condition in the equatorial plane after substituting u^t = E/(1 - 2M/r) and u^phi = L/r^2.
key_equations.symbols: E-tilde, L-tilde conserved energy and angular momentum (OCR shows bars)

key_equations.name: Photon effective-energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Radial motion of light is a particle of energy 1/b^2 moving in the potential W_eff.
key_equations.symbols: b impact parameter; W_eff photon effective potential

key_equations.name: Definition of b
key_equations.meaning: The single constant that fixes a photon trajectory; the effective energy is 1/b^2.
key_equations.symbols: script E effective energy

key_equations.name: Photon effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Potential hill seen by every photon; it has no angular-momentum dependence.
key_equations.symbols: M mass in geometrized units

key_equations.name: b far from the mass
key_equations.meaning: For r much larger than 2M the redshift factor is 1, so b reduces to r^2 dphi/dt.

key_equations.name: Angular rate of a distant straight ray
key_equations.meaning: Using phi ~ d/r and dr/dt ~ -1 for an incoming ray at offset d; combined with 24.8 gives b = d.
key_equations.symbols: d perpendicular offset of the ray

key_equations.name: Impact parameter identification
key_equations.meaning: The ratio L/E is the geometric impact parameter of a ray from infinity.

key_equations.name: Peak of the photon potential
key_equations.meaning: Location and height of the barrier; also the radius of the unstable photon sphere.
key_equations.symbols: r_0 radius of the maximum (not the r_0 of Chapter 23)

key_equations.name: Scattering versus capture criterion
key_equations.meaning: Classification of incoming rays by comparing their energy level with the barrier height.
Trajectory shape from the ratio of tangent components.
Null condition in the equatorial plane with theta fixed.
Null condition divided by (u^phi)^2.

key_equations.name: Index rearrangement (margin note 5)
key_equations.meaning: Lowering indices with the diagonal metric exposes the conserved components u_t and u_phi, whose ratio is 1/b.
Shape equation in r; simplifies to r^4/b^2 - r^2(1 - 2M/r).
Shape equation after substituting u = M/r.

key_equations.name: First integral of the photon orbit
key_equations.meaning: Energy-like first integral for the ray shape; turning points where the right side vanishes.
key_equations.symbols: u = M/r

key_equations.name: Photon orbit equation
key_equations.meaning: Differentiated form; the 3u^2 term is the entire relativistic correction to straight-line motion.

key_equations.name: Newtonian limit for light
key_equations.meaning: Massless limit of the Newtonian orbit equation (eqn 20.33): straight lines.
key_equations.symbols: primes denote d/dphi

key_equations.name: Zeroth-order straight line
key_equations.meaning: Undeflected ray at distance b from the mass, valid when M/b is small.
Linearized equation for the first correction, sourced by the zeroth-order solution.
Same source written as a constant plus a cos 2phi term.
Particular solution: a constant 3/2 (M/b)^2 plus (1/2)(M/b)^2 cos 2phi.

key_equations.name: Perturbed light-ray trajectory
key_equations.meaning: Trajectory accurate to second order in M/b.

key_equations.name: Asymptote condition (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Condition u = 0 for the directions of the incoming and outgoing asymptotes. The printed equation has (3 + 2 cos phi); dividing eqn 24.21 by M/b gives (3 + cos 2phi), which is what yields the quoted roots.

key_equations.name: Deflection angle
key_equations.meaning: Each asymptote is rotated by 2M/b beyond the straight-line value, giving a total deflection 4M/b.
key_equations.symbols: The book writes Delta phi for the deflection here.

key_equations.name: Solar light deflection
key_equations.meaning: Deflection of a ray grazing the Sun, with b = 6.9e8 m; twice the Newtonian corpuscular value.
key_equations.symbols: G gravitational constant, c speed of light, M solar mass

key_equations.name: Focal distance of a point-mass lens
key_equations.meaning: Distance behind the mass at which a parallel ray with impact parameter b meets the axis; depends on b, so no single focus.
key_equations.symbols: D distance from lens to crossing point; theta = 4M/b

key_equations.name: Photon momentum in flat spacetime
key_equations.meaning: Starting point recalled for Section 24.2.
key_equations.symbols: E photon energy

key_equations.meaning: Massive momentum expressed via coordinate velocity.
Conserved energy per unit mass used to eliminate u^t.
Momentum in terms of E-tilde.

key_equations.name: Momentum at fixed energy at infinity
key_equations.meaning: Form that survives m -> 0 with epsilon = m E-tilde held fixed; used to define photon momentum.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon energy at infinity

key_equations.meaning: Coordinate components in terms of coordinate velocities.

key_equations.name: b in coordinate time
key_equations.meaning: Impact parameter expressed with coordinate time, valid at any r.
Null condition divided by dt^2.
Same condition with dphi/dt replaced by b, fixing dr/dt.

key_equations.name: Photon momentum components
key_equations.meaning: Complete coordinate momentum of an equatorial photon labelled by epsilon and b; the sign of p^r marks outgoing or ingoing.

key_equations.name: Emission angle in the local frame
key_equations.meaning: Sine of the angle from the radial direction equals the sideways velocity in the static observer's orthonormal frame.
key_equations.symbols: hats denote orthonormal-frame components

key_equations.meaning: Vielbein conversion of coordinate components.
key_equations.symbols: (e_mu)^nu-hat vielbein components

key_equations.name: Static-frame vielbeins (margin note 9)
key_equations.meaning: Components for theta = pi/2 used to convert photon momentum into what a static observer measures.

key_equations.name: Emission angle formula
key_equations.meaning: Relates the locally measured angle to the conserved impact parameter.

key_equations.name: Critical emission angle
key_equations.meaning: Boundary between escaping and captured emission directions; sin psi_c = 1 at r = 3M and 0 at r = 2M (obtuse branch outside 3M, acute inside).

key_equations.name: Summary table: massive radial rate (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Massive-particle entry of the summary table; the printed table has L-tilde/r^2 where L-tilde^2/r^2 is required.

key_equations.name: Summary table: massive coordinate-time rates
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-time velocities for massive equatorial motion.
key_equations.symbols: E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau, L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dtau

key_equations.name: Summary table: photon coordinate-time rates
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-time velocities for light. Our check (not stated in the book): the massive rows reduce to these when E-tilde and L-tilde grow at fixed ratio b.

key_equations.name: Point-mass lens equation
key_equations.latex: \theta_{\rm i}=\theta_{\rm s}+\frac{\theta_{\rm E}^2}{\theta_{\rm i}},\qquad\theta_{\rm E}^2=\frac{4MD_{\ell s}}{D_\ell D_s}
key_equations.meaning: Small-angle relation between image and source directions (Exercise 24.3).
key_equations.symbols: theta_i image angle, theta_s source angle, D_l, D_s, D_ls distances

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element
key_equations.meaning: Cosmological metric for Exercise 24.4.
key_equations.symbols: a(t) scale factor, k curvature constant

key_equations.meaning: Radial-ray reduction with chi a function of r only.
Conserved-component result for a radial light ray in an expanding universe.
key_equations.symbols: C constant

key_equations.name: Affine parameter along a cosmological ray
key_equations.meaning: Affine parameter accumulates as a^2 times comoving distance, with t evaluated along the ray.

figures.label: Fig. 24.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Construction used to define the impact parameter of a light ray.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing with a vertical y-axis and horizontal x-axis meeting at a black dot labelled M. A curved ray enters from the right, running horizontally at some height above the x-axis with a leftward arrowhead, then bends downward past the y-axis and leaves towards the lower left with an arrowhead. A straight segment joins M to the point where the ray is still horizontal on the right, making an angle phi with the x-axis, and a vertical double-headed arrow labelled d marks the height of the ray above the x-axis at that point.
figures.what_it_teaches: A far-away ray is a straight line at perpendicular offset d, so the angle phi is about d/r there; this is the geometry behind showing L/E equals d.

redesign.idea: Draggable ray launcher: a stream of parallel rays approaches a mass; the learner picks one and sees d, phi and r update live while a readout compares r^2 dphi/dt with L/E computed from the integrated geodesic.
redesign.interaction: Drag the launch height d and the mass M; toggle between flat space and Schwarzschild; hover along the ray to see local values.

figures.label: Fig. 24.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: The effective potential that governs photon motion in Schwarzschild spacetime.
figures.visual_description: Plot with vertical axis labelled W_eff(r-vector) and horizontal axis labelled |r-vector|, with a 0 marked where the horizontal axis crosses. The curve rises almost vertically from far below the axis at small radius, crosses zero, reaches a single sharp peak a short distance to the right, and then decays smoothly towards zero at large radius. No radii or values are marked.
figures.what_it_teaches: Light sees a single barrier and no well: rays below the peak bounce off, rays above it plunge inward, and the peak is an unstable balance point (the photon sphere).

redesign.idea: Potential-plus-orbit twin view: the W_eff curve on the left with a horizontal energy line at 1/b^2, and the resulting ray around the mass on the right, with r = 2M and r = 3M marked on both.
redesign.interaction: Slide b (or 1/b^2) through the critical value sqrt(27) M; the energy line moves, the turning point marker appears or vanishes, and the ray flips between scattering, whirling near 3M, and plunging.

figures.label: Fig. 24.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Angles used in computing how much a photon is deflected.
figures.visual_description: Axes y (vertical) and x (horizontal) with the origin at the mass. A ray arrives from the right at height b (double-headed vertical arrow labelled b) with a leftward arrowhead, curves around above the origin and heads down to the lower left with an arrowhead. A straight line from the origin to the incoming ray makes angle phi with the x-axis. A large arc labelled Delta phi sweeps from the incoming direction around to the outgoing asymptote, and a dotted straight line continues down-left from the origin; the small angle between this dotted line and the outgoing branch is labelled delta phi.
figures.what_it_teaches: The total turn of the ray is the extra angle beyond a straight half-turn; the asymptotes are where 1/r goes to zero.

redesign.idea: Exact versus perturbative deflection: numerically integrate u'' + u = 3u^2 and overlay the first-order trajectory 24.21 and the straight line, with the asymptote angles drawn and a live plot of deflection against M/b showing where 4M/b fails.
redesign.interaction: Slider for M/b from 1e-6 (solar) to near 1/sqrt(27); zoom control to magnify tiny solar deflections; readout of exact, first-order and Newtonian (2M/b) values.

figures.label: Fig. 24.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A common rubber-sheet cartoon of starlight being bent by the Sun's curved space.
figures.visual_description: Perspective view of a square wire-mesh sheet with a small dimple in which a white ball (the Sun) sits. Two small circles hover above the far edge, labelled 'Actual star' and 'Image of star'. A curved line from the near side of the sheet passes close to the ball and bends up towards the actual star, while a straight line from the same viewing region extends back to the image position, so the image appears displaced away from the Sun.
figures.what_it_teaches: Starlight passing the Sun arrives from a slightly different direction, so the star appears pushed outward from the Sun.

redesign.idea: Replace the rubber sheet with an eclipse sky simulator: a star field around the eclipsed Sun where each star is displaced radially by 4M/b, exaggerated by a zoom factor, alongside a split bar showing half the effect from g_tt and half from spatial curvature.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'time part only', 'space part only' and 'full GR'; adjust the exaggeration factor; compare with the Newtonian-corpuscle pattern.

figures.label: Fig. 24.5(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Rays bent by a mass do not come to a single focus.
figures.visual_description: Vertical ray diagram. Two pairs of parallel vertical lines come down from the top, symmetric about a central axis on which a dot labelled ell (the lens) sits. The inner pair, at horizontal distance b from the axis (arrow labelled b from ell), kink inward at the level of the lens and meet on the axis at a point a distance D below it, with the angle theta marked between the axis and the converging ray. The outer pair kinks inward at the same height but less steeply and meets the axis at a lower point.
figures.what_it_teaches: Because the deflection falls off as 1/b, outer rays cross the axis farther away (D = b^2/4M), so a point mass has a focal line rather than a focal point.

redesign.idea: Glass lens versus gravity lens: side-by-side ray bundles through an ideal convex lens and past a point mass, with crossing points plotted on the axis and a D-versus-b graph.
redesign.interaction: Drag the mass, add rays at chosen b, switch between lens types; a screen can be slid along the axis to show the ring-like caustic pattern.

figures.label: Fig. 24.5(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: An Einstein ring: rays from a source bent around a mass reach the observer, who traces them back along straight lines to a ring in the source plane.
figures.visual_description: A cone drawn in perspective with its apex at the bottom labelled O (observer) and an ellipse at the top standing for a circle in the source plane; the source point s sits at the centre of that ellipse. A dot labelled ell lies on the cone's axis roughly halfway up. Two curved rays bow outward from s, pass on either side of ell and reconverge at O, while the straight sides of the cone are the observer's back-extended lines of sight that land on the rim of the ellipse, i.e. the ring image.
figures.what_it_teaches: With perfect alignment the same deflection happens in every azimuth, so the apparent images form a circle around the lens.

redesign.idea: 3D lensing sandbox: a source, lens and observer on an optical bench with the observer's sky rendered as an image; the ring appears when aligned and breaks into two arcs when the source is moved off axis, with theta_E indicated.
redesign.interaction: Drag the source transversely and change the distances D_l, D_s; orbit the 3D camera to see the cone of rays.

figures.label: Fig. 24.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Construction for photons sent out from a point at radius r.
figures.visual_description: At the top, an emission point with local axes: z pointing up (away from the mass) and x pointing right. A dashed vertical line of length r runs down to the origin (the mass) near the bottom. A solid straight line leaves the emission point heading down and to the right, continuing as a dashed line; the angle psi is marked by an arc from the z-axis round to this line, so psi is larger than a right angle. A dashed segment labelled b runs from the origin perpendicular to that line, with a right-angle mark, and another dashed line through the origin runs parallel to it. A thick curve leaves the emission point on the same initial heading but bends back and winds around the origin in a tightening spiral.
figures.what_it_teaches: In flat space the offset of a straight line from the origin is r sin psi; a ray with small enough b, launched inward, instead spirals into the mass.

redesign.idea: Lighthouse at radius r: a static emitter fires a fan of rays in all directions, drawn as exact null geodesics coloured escape (gold) or capture (dark), with the critical cone and its angle psi_c shown in the emitter's local frame.
redesign.interaction: Drag the emitter from 20M down to just above 2M; watch the capture cone widen through half the sky at 3M; readouts of psi_c and captured sky fraction (about 6 percent at 10M, 15 percent at 6M, 50 percent at 3M).

figures.label: Fig. 24.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A photon whose 1/b^2 lies above the peak of W_eff falls all the way in.
figures.visual_description: Same W_eff(r-vector) against |r-vector| curve as Fig. 24.2, now with the peak position marked r_0 on the horizontal axis by a dotted vertical line and the peak height marked by a dotted horizontal line carrying the label 1/b^2 on the vertical axis. Higher up, above the peak, a long horizontal arrow points left toward small radius, indicating a photon whose level clears the barrier.
figures.what_it_teaches: An incoming ray whose energy level clears the barrier at r_0 never meets a turning point and is captured.

redesign.idea: Merge into the Fig. 24.2 twin view as a capture preset: the energy line animates leftward over the hill while the paired orbit panel shows the ray winding in.
redesign.interaction: Play/pause the animation; nudge 1/b^2 just above and below the peak to see near-critical rays whirl many times around 3M before deciding.

figures.label: Fig. 24.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lensing ray diagram for Exercise 24.3 with source s, lens ell and observer O.
figures.visual_description: Three vertical lines mark the source plane (left, containing point s), the lens plane (middle, containing a dot ell slightly below the s-O line) and the observer (right, point O). A dotted horizontal line joins s to O and another dotted line from O passes through ell to the lower left. A ray leaves s upward to the lens plane above ell, bends there by angle alpha and runs to O; its straight back-extension from O reaches the source plane higher up. A second ray from s goes below ell and on to O, with its back-extension to the lower part of the source plane. At O the angles theta_i and theta_s are marked from the O-ell line. On the left, vertical arrows mark the transverse lengths theta_i D_s, alpha D_ls and theta_s D_s; along the bottom, arrows mark D_ls (source to lens), D_l (lens to observer) and D_s (source to observer).
figures.what_it_teaches: Adding transverse offsets in the source plane gives theta_i D_s = theta_s D_s + alpha D_ls, which with alpha = 4M/(theta_i D_l) becomes the lens equation.

redesign.idea: Lens-equation solver: a draggable source on the bench with the two image angles computed from theta_i = theta_s + theta_E^2/theta_i and shown both on the ray diagram and as a sky view with brightness weights.
redesign.interaction: Drag theta_s and the three distances; watch the images approach the Einstein circle as theta_s -> 0.

figures.label: Chapter summary table (p. 260)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Reference table of equatorial motion in Schwarzschild spacetime for massive particles and for photons.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked ruled tables with no caption. The upper block, headed 'Massive particles', has rows for the useful constants E-tilde and L-tilde, then dr/dtau, dr/dt and dphi/dt. The lower block, headed 'Photons', has a row for the constant b = L/E written with coordinate time, then dr/dt and dphi/dt. Each right-hand cell holds a formula with factors of (1 - 2M/r).
figures.what_it_teaches: Massless motion is the limit of massive motion with only the ratio b surviving, and coordinate-time rates all carry the (1 - 2M/r) slowdown factor.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

redesign.idea: Morphing formula card: a slider sends the particle mass to zero at fixed epsilon so each massive formula visibly collapses to the photon row, with a live trajectory preview.
redesign.interaction: Slide m/epsilon to zero; hover over each factor to see its physical meaning.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.1
worked_examples.problem: Give a qualitative reason why gravity should affect the path of light at all.
worked_examples.method: Apply the null condition to a static diagonal metric to find the coordinate speed of light, relate g_00 to the potential, and state the Fermat-type variational principle with g_ij/(-g_00).
worked_examples.key_insight: Since coordinate light speed varies from place to place, space acts like an inhomogeneous optical medium, so a spacetime null geodesic can project onto a bent spatial path.
worked_examples.result: c'^2 = -c^2 g_00 (for the spatial metric along the path) and delta integral of sqrt(g_ij dx^i dx^j/(-g_00)) = 0.
concepts: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime

worked_examples.label: Example 24.2
worked_examples.problem: Interpret the constant b = L-tilde/E-tilde geometrically.
worked_examples.method: Take a ray travelling parallel to the x-axis at offset d; far away the redshift factor is 1 so b = r^2 dphi/dt; use phi ~ d/r and dr/dt ~ -1.
worked_examples.key_insight: The ratio of the two conserved quantities is the impact parameter, so the energy-like quantity 1/b^2 is fixed by geometry alone.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

worked_examples.label: Reading the photon potential (embedded in 24.1)
worked_examples.problem: Use W_eff to classify the possible fates of light rays and find where light can orbit.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate W_eff to find its peak; compare the energy level 1/b^2 with the peak height; note the lack of a minimum.
worked_examples.key_insight: A single barrier with no well means scattering or capture but never stable light orbits; the balance point at 3M is unstable.
worked_examples.result: r0 = 3M, W_eff(r0) = 1/(27M^2); b > sqrt(27) M deflected, b < sqrt(27) M captured, b = sqrt(27) M unstable circular orbit.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.3
worked_examples.problem: Derive the shape equation for equatorial light rays in Schwarzschild spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Write dr/dphi = u^r/u^phi, divide the null condition by (u^phi)^2, rewrite the time term with lowered components to insert 1/b^2, substitute u = M/r, simplify, and differentiate with respect to phi.
worked_examples.key_insight: The photon orbit equation differs from the Newtonian straight-line equation only by the source term 3u^2.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.4
worked_examples.problem: Find the path of a ray that passes far from the mass (M/b small) and its total deflection.
worked_examples.method: Expand about u0 = (M/b) sin phi, solve u1'' + u1 = 3u0^2 with a constant plus cos 2phi, then set u = 0 and solve for phi near 0 and pi to first order; the text following the box extracts the angle.
worked_examples.key_insight: Each end of the trajectory is rotated by 2M/b beyond the straight-line asymptote, so the deflection is 4M/b and independent of photon energy.
worked_examples.result: u ~ (M/b) sin phi + (1/2)(M/b)^2 (3 + cos 2phi); asymptotes at phi ~ -2M/b and pi + 2M/b; deflection 4M/b.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.5
worked_examples.problem: Evaluate the deflection of starlight that just grazes the Sun and connect it with observations.
worked_examples.method: Restore G and c in 4M/b, insert the solar mass and b = 6.9e8 m, convert radians to arcseconds, and compare with Soldner's Newtonian estimate.
worked_examples.key_insight: The GR prediction is about twice the Newtonian corpuscular value, which is what made an eclipse measurement decisive in principle.
worked_examples.result: About 8.6e-6 rad, roughly 1.8 arcsec; tested by the 1919 eclipse and confirmed precisely by radio sources.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.6
worked_examples.problem: Decide whether a point mass focuses parallel light like a lens.
worked_examples.method: For a ray at impact parameter b, use the small-angle crossing distance D = b/theta with theta = 4M/b.
worked_examples.key_insight: The crossing distance grows as b^2, so there is no common focus; the analogy with a lens breaks down.

worked_examples.label: Example 24.7
worked_examples.problem: Construct the components of a photon's four-momentum in Schwarzschild coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Write massive p^mu in terms of coordinate velocity and u^t, replace u^t with E-tilde, define epsilon = m E-tilde, take m -> 0; then express dphi/dt with b and solve the null condition divided by dt^2 for dr/dt.
worked_examples.key_insight: Holding the energy at infinity fixed gives a finite massless limit, and the whole momentum is fixed by epsilon and b.
worked_examples.result: p^t = epsilon/(1 - 2M/r), p^r = +/- epsilon [1 - (b^2/r^2)(1 - 2M/r)]^{1/2}, p^theta = 0, p^phi = epsilon b/r^2.

worked_examples.label: Critical emission angle (embedded in 24.2)
worked_examples.problem: Find the range of directions in which a static emitter at radius r can send light that escapes.
worked_examples.method: Define sin psi as the ratio of orthonormal phi and t momentum components, convert with static vielbeins, insert eqn 24.32, then set b = sqrt(27) M.
worked_examples.key_insight: The locally measured angle is tied to the conserved b by sin psi = (b/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}, so the capture threshold in b becomes a cone of directions that widens as r decreases.
worked_examples.result: sin psi_c = (sqrt(27) M/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}; psi_c = 90 degrees at r = 3M and all light captured as r -> 2M.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A gravitational field as a medium with a position-dependent refractive index, with rays obeying a least-time principle
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 24.1 notes the coordinate light speed depends on g_00, likens this to refraction, and states a Fermat principle so that bending seems natural before any geodesic is solved.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only works for static spacetimes and coordinate speeds; the local speed is always c. Using g_00 alone gives half the true deflection; the spatial metric must be included in the index.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Graded-index optics sandbox: a ray in a medium with n(r) = 1/sqrt(-g_00) versus n(r) from the full isotropic metric, overlaid on the true null geodesic, showing the factor of two.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A photon as a particle with energy 1/b^2 rolling toward a potential hill W_eff
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The chapter maps the null condition onto the familiar energy-plus-potential picture so turning points, capture and unstable circular orbits are read off a plot.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'energy' is geometric (an inverse impact parameter squared), the 'time' is the affine parameter, and nothing about the photon's actual energy enters.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball-on-hill animation synchronized with the actual ray around the mass.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Light orbiting on the photon sphere is like a ball balanced on a hilltop
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Because circular photon orbits sit at the maximum of W_eff, the text concludes they are unstable, just as for the massive-particle maximum.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real near-critical rays wind around several times before leaving; the instability grows exponentially in the number of orbits, which the ball picture does not quantify.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Nudge a photon off the 3M circle by a tiny amount and count laps before escape or capture.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Impact parameter as angular momentum per unit energy, with more energetic projectiles scattered less
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used right after Example 24.2 to make b = L/E feel physically sensible.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: For photons L scales with energy, so b is purely geometric and deflection does not depend on photon energy; the scattering-by-energy intuition belongs to massive particles.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A gravitating mass as a lens
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Introduced and immediately tested: the crossing distance D = b^2/4M shows there is no focus, so the analogy is only partial; the aligned case gives a ring.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: No single focal length; image positions obey the lens equation rather than the thin-lens formula; magnification and caustics differ from glass optics.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Wine-glass-foot lens comparison: photograph-like rendering of a background grid seen through a point-mass lens versus a convex lens.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rubber-sheet picture of starlight bending around the Sun (Fig. 24.4)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offered as a familiar way the effect is illustrated, after the eclipse discussion.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Shows only curved space; half the deflection comes from the time part of the metric, and a sheet embedded in a gravitating room smuggles in the gravity it claims to explain.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between rubber-sheet cartoon and a decomposition bar showing space and time contributions of 2M/b each.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Running the film backwards: rays that an emitter would lose into the hole correspond to directions from which an observer receives nothing
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: time-reversal symmetry of a static spacetime
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Closes Section 24.2 by turning the capture cone for emitted photons into a black region in the observer's sky.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Assumes a static geometry and that nothing inside the photon sphere emits light; for collapsing stars or rotating holes the argument must be refined.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between emission mode (arrows outward from the observer) and reception mode (arrows inward) with the same cone shaded black.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Light is massless, so gravity cannot bend it.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR light follows null geodesics of curved spacetime and is deflected by 4M/b; even Newtonian corpuscular reasoning gives a nonzero (half-size) effect.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian force is proportional to mass, and in the book's own Newtonian orbit chapter photons move in straight lines.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because a light ray follows a geodesic, its path through space must be straight.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A geodesic of spacetime projected into space need not be a spatial geodesic; in a static field the spatial path follows the optical metric g_ij/(-g_00).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Geodesics are introduced as the curved-space version of straight lines.
concepts: Fermat's principle in a static spacetime

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The conserved energy and angular momentum defined with proper time do not apply to photons.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They follow from the metric's symmetries and hold along any geodesic with an affine parameter, null ones included.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Earlier definitions used d/dtau, which is undefined for light.
concepts: conserved energy and angular momentum along null geodesics

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Light can orbit a compact mass stably, like a planet.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: W_eff has no minimum; the only circular light orbits are at the peak r = 3M and are unstable.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Massive particles have stable circular orbits, and the photon sphere is often drawn as a neat ring of light.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Rays with different angular momenta see different effective potentials, as massive particles do.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: After scaling by L^2, W_eff is the same function for every photon; only the level 1/b^2 changes.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: V_eff for massive particles changes shape with L-tilde.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A gravitational lens brings light to a focus just like a glass lens.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The crossing distance D = b^2/4M depends on impact parameter, so there is no single focus; aligned systems produce rings and off-axis ones produce multiple images.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name 'gravitational lens' and pictures of converging rays.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: GR merely reproduces the Newtonian prediction for light bending.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: GR predicts about twice Soldner's corpuscular value (1.75 versus about 0.87 arcsec at the solar limb), which is what the eclipse test discriminated.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In the perihelion and redshift tests the Newtonian limit is the leading behaviour, and for slow particles GR and Newton agree.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Eddington's 1919 eclipse data settled the question cleanly and precisely.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The measurement agreed with GR within its estimated errors, but later analyses questioned its systematics; precise confirmation came from later radio measurements.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The expedition is told as a triumphant turning point that made Einstein famous.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Higher-energy (bluer) photons are deflected less because they scatter less.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The trajectory depends only on b = L/E; the deflection 4M/b is the same for all frequencies, as the equivalence principle requires.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text's remark that b decreases with energy borrows an intuition from massive-particle scattering.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The rubber-sheet picture of curved space accounts for the full bending of starlight.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: At first order the time part of the metric (g_tt) and spatial curvature (g_rr) each contribute 2M/b; a picture of curved space alone captures only half.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Fig. 24.4 is captioned as curved space bending starlight, and rubber sheets are ubiquitous in popular accounts.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The speed of light really changes near a mass.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the coordinate speed varies; every local observer using their own rods and clocks measures c.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Example 24.1 speaks of a varying speed of light and a refractive index.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any photon emitted with b below sqrt(27) M falls into the mass, whatever its direction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Outside r = 3M an outward-directed photon escapes for any b; capture requires b < sqrt(27) M and an inward heading, which is why the critical angle is obtuse there. Inside 3M outward rays with large b turn back.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text states the capture criterion 1/b^2 > W(r0) without mentioning the direction, and sin psi does not distinguish psi from pi - psi.

thought_experiments.name: Stars next to the eclipsed Sun
thought_experiments.setup: Photograph a star field during a total solar eclipse and again at night months later, and compare positions of stars whose light passed near the solar limb.
thought_experiments.lesson: Light passing the Sun is deflected, so stars appear pushed radially outward by up to about 1.75 arcsec, twice the Newtonian corpuscular value.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Blink comparator between eclipse and night images with exaggerated displacement vectors scaling as 1/b.

thought_experiments.name: Parallel beam past a point mass
thought_experiments.setup: Send a wide parallel beam of light past a single compact mass and look for where the rays cross the axis.
thought_experiments.lesson: Each ring of rays crosses at its own distance b^2/4M, so the mass is a lens without a focus.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Slide a screen along the axis behind the mass and watch the illuminated ring shrink and grow.

thought_experiments.name: Perfect alignment of source, lens and observer
thought_experiments.setup: Place a distant source exactly behind a compact mass as seen by the observer.
thought_experiments.lesson: Symmetry turns the two images into a ring whose angular radius is the Einstein angle.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drag the source through alignment and see arcs merge into a ring.

thought_experiments.name: A lamp hovering at radius r
thought_experiments.setup: A static observer at fixed r emits photons uniformly in all directions and records which ones reach infinity; repeat for smaller r.
thought_experiments.lesson: Beyond a critical angle photons are captured; the captured fraction grows from a few percent far away to half the sky at r = 3M and all of it as r -> 2M.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Lighthouse simulation with shaded escape cone and captured-fraction readout.

thought_experiments.name: Playing the lamp film backwards
thought_experiments.setup: Reverse the emitter experiment in time: the static observer now receives light from all directions.
thought_experiments.lesson: Directions inside the capture cone trace back into the hole, so no light arrives from them and that region of sky is black.
concepts: time-reversal symmetry of a static spacetime
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ray-traced sky view for a hovering observer against a star background, with the dark disk growing as the observer descends.

historical_notes.event: Treated light as Newtonian corpuscles falling in the Sun's field and estimated an apparent displacement of roughly 0.8 arcsec for stars seen next to the solar limb (his paper dates from the early 1800s; the book gives only his life dates, 1776-1833).
historical_notes.significance: Shows light bending was anticipated classically, and supplies the Newtonian value that GR doubles.

historical_notes.event: Earlier, largely neglected speculations about gravity acting on light; Michell is also credited with first proposing black holes, explaining double stars gravitationally and bringing statistics into cosmology.
historical_notes.significance: Places the GR prediction in a longer tradition and foreshadows the dark stars of the black-hole chapters.

historical_notes.event: Eclipse expedition measured shifts of star positions near the Sun, finding agreement with the GR prediction within the estimated uncertainties.
historical_notes.significance: Made Einstein a public celebrity; the book notes that later analyses questioned the systematic errors and points to Earman and Glymour (1980).

historical_notes.event: Later high-precision measurements of the deflection of radio sources near the Sun.
historical_notes.significance: Provide the robust confirmation of the GR value that the eclipse plates could not.

applications_and_observations.topic: Deflection of starlight grazing the Sun
applications_and_observations.details: 4GM/(c^2 b) evaluated at the solar limb; the book uses b = 6.9e8 m and quotes the solar radius as about 696,000 km.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: 8.6e-6 rad, about 1.8 arcsec. Our check: GM_sun/c^2 = 1477 m, R_sun = 6.957e8 m gives 8.49e-6 rad = 1.75 arcsec.

applications_and_observations.details: Corpuscular Newtonian light bending, half the GR value.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: around 0.8 arcsec; exact half of the GR limb value is 0.875 arcsec (our figure).

applications_and_observations.details: Star positions near the eclipsed Sun compared with night-time positions; agreed with GR within estimated uncertainties, systematics later questioned.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Not given in the book. Commonly quoted results (external): about 1.98 arcsec from Sobral and 1.61 arcsec from Principe, each with uncertainties of order 0.1-0.3 arcsec.

applications_and_observations.details: Very-long-baseline radio interferometry of quasars passing near the Sun confirms the GR deflection with high precision.
