applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Not given in the book. External context: VLBI analyses constrain the PPN parameter gamma to about 1 part in 10^4 of the GR value.

applications_and_observations.topic: Photon sphere and critical impact parameter
applications_and_observations.details: Circular light orbits at 3M require b = sqrt(27) M. Our estimate: for the Sun 3M is 4.4 km and for a 1.4 solar-mass neutron star 6.2 km, both inside the bodies, so photon spheres need objects more compact than about 3M, in practice black holes.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: r = 3M; b_c = sqrt(27) M = 5.196 M; W_eff peak 1/(27 M^2). Our figures: 3M_sun = 4.4 km; 3(1.4 M_sun) = 6.2 km.

applications_and_observations.topic: Focal distance of the Sun as a gravitational lens
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate using D = b^2/4M with b at least the solar radius: rays grazing the limb meet the axis around 550 AU from the Sun, and rays with larger b meet farther out, forming a focal line; this is the basis of proposed solar-gravitational-lens telescope missions.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our computation: R_sun^2/(4 GM_sun/c^2) = 8.2e13 m, about 548 AU.

applications_and_observations.details: Einstein angle from Exercise 24.3. Our estimate for a solar-mass star 4 kpc away lensing a source at 8 kpc gives a ring of angular radius about a milliarcsecond, unresolvable, so such events are seen as brightening (microlensing); galaxy-mass lenses give arcsecond rings seen in telescope images.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our computation: theta_E = sqrt(4GM D_ls/(c^2 D_l D_s)) = 1.0 mas (ring radius; diameter about 2 mas) for M = M_sun, D_l = 4 kpc, D_s = 8 kpc.

applications_and_observations.topic: Captured fraction of light emitted by a static observer
applications_and_observations.details: Our evaluation of sin psi_c = (sqrt(27) M/r)(1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}, choosing the obtuse branch outside 3M, with captured solid-angle fraction (1 + cos psi_c)/2.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our computation: r = 10M psi_c = 152 deg, 5.7 percent captured; 6M 135 deg, 14.6 percent; 4M 113 deg, 30 percent; 3M 90 deg, 50 percent; 2.5M 68 deg, 68 percent; 2.2M 45 deg, 85 percent; 2M all captured.

applications_and_observations.details: For a distant observer the dark region has angular radius about sqrt(27) M/D, set by the critical impact parameter rather than by 2M. Our estimates for the EHT targets; the book shows the Sgr A* image in the next chapter (Fig. 25.1).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our computation: shadow diameter 2 sqrt(27) GM/(c^2 D) is about 40 microarcsec for M87* (6.5e9 M_sun, 16.8 Mpc) and about 50 microarcsec for Sgr A* (4.0e6 M_sun, 8.28 kpc); EHT ring diameters were reported as about 42 and 52 microarcsec (external).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized G = c = 1 with M standing for GM/c^2; constants restored in Example 24.5 (4GM/c^2 b). Example 24.1 keeps an explicit c.
(-, +, +, +); photons satisfy u.u = 0 and massive particles u.u = -1.
E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dlambda and L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dlambda for photons (dtau for massive particles, per unit rest mass).
notation_and_conventions.notes: The OCR copy renders the tildes as bars in several places.

notation_and_conventions.convention: b = L-tilde/E-tilde; the effective energy is script E = 1/b^2; script T = (dr/dlambda)^2/L-tilde^2 is the kinetic-like term.

W_eff(r) = (1 - 2M/r)/r^2 is the photon potential; V_eff is reserved for massive particles. The text sometimes drops the subscript and writes W(r0). Plots label the axes W_eff(r-vector) and |r-vector|.
Here r0 = 3M is the location of the maximum of W_eff.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In Chapter 23 r0 denoted a circular-orbit or orbital radius; do not carry that meaning over.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Bold u is the tangent (four-velocity) vector; plain u = M/r (dimensionless) in the orbit equation, and u = 1/r in margin note 1; primes mean d/dphi; u0 and u1 are zeroth- and first-order parts of u.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Triple use of the same letter in two pages.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Fig. 24.3 labels the total swept angle Delta phi and the deflection delta phi; the text and eqn 24.23 call the deflection Delta phi.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Treat 4M/b as the deflection whichever symbol is used.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Script epsilon = m E-tilde, the energy measured far away; kept finite as m -> 0 for photons.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Distinct from script E (effective energy) and from the eccentricity epsilon of Chapter 23.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Hats mark components in an orthonormal (static observer) frame; (e_mu)^nu-hat are vielbein components converting coordinate components to hatted ones.
Measured in the emitter's local frame from the outward radial direction (the z-axis of Fig. 24.6); psi_c is the critical value.

s source, ell lens, O observer; D_l observer-lens, D_s observer-source, D_ls lens-source distances; theta_i image angle, theta_s source angle, theta_E Einstein angle, alpha deflection; in Example 24.6 theta is the deflection and D the axis-crossing distance.

Biographical note on Soldner, plus mention that Cavendish, Michell and Newton also considered gravity acting on light; Michell is praised as an unsung pioneer who first suggested black holes, explained binary stars by gravity and used statistics in cosmology.

Explains that E-tilde and L-tilde came from geometry (symmetry) in the previous chapter, so they hold for photons even though proper time cannot be used.
Shows the index gymnastics that turn g_tt (u^t)^2/(u^phi)^2 into an expression with lowered components, so that 1/b^2 can be inserted.
Quotes the solar radius as roughly 696,000 km for the grazing-ray estimate.
Points to Earman and Glymour (1980) in Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences for the history of the 1919 eclipse measurements.
Says the consequences of the Einstein ring geometry are worked out in the exercises.
Lists the static-observer vielbein components in the equatorial plane used to convert photon momentum into local components.
Italic closing remark to Exercise 24.4: tracking the affine parameter along a geodesic is a handy tool, with Exercise 26.4 cited as a place it gets used.

difficulty.notes: Algebra is light for readers who did Chapters 22-23, since each step mirrors the massive case, and the perturbative deflection uses only a forced oscillator. The text has several slips (eqn 24.22, margin note 3, the massive dr/dtau entry of the summary table, inconsistent Delta phi labelling) and leaves lensing mostly to exercises.

teaching_gems.gem: Rename rather than re-derive: the photon energy equation is the massive one with 1/b^2 as energy and W_eff as potential.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners transfer intuition about turning points, capture and unstable orbits directly, and the only new thing to absorb is the shape of one curve.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side V_eff (with L slider) and W_eff (no slider) panels, highlighting that the photon curve never changes shape while the energy line moves.

teaching_gems.gem: All the relativistic bending of light lives in one term: u'' + u = 3u^2 against the Newtonian u'' + u = 0.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Isolating the correction makes it clear what GR adds and prepares a clean perturbation argument.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Coefficient dial on the right-hand side (0 to 3 u^2, or 2 u^2 for a 'space only' toy) with ray traces updating live.

teaching_gems.gem: Get the deflection without integrals: perturb a straight line and read off where 1/r vanishes.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The asymptote trick turns a global question into a local root-finding step accessible to anyone who can solve a forced oscillator.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot u(phi) for u0 and u0 + u1 with the two zero crossings highlighted and their shifts labelled 2M/b.

teaching_gems.gem: The factor of two over Soldner is the whole point of the eclipse test.
teaching_gems.why_effective: It gives a concrete, falsifiable number contrast and a story with an honest epistemic caveat about the 1919 data.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Eclipse data playground: plot mock star displacements with error bars against 1/b and fit Newtonian versus GR slopes.

teaching_gems.gem: Test the analogy you just offered: D = b^2/4M shows a mass is a lens with no focus.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 24.22 has (3 + 2 cos phi); setting eqn 24.21 to zero gives (3 + cos 2phi).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: With the printed form the roots come out as -5M/(2b), contradicting the stated -2M/b and the 4M/b result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use 2 sin phi = -(M/b)(3 + cos 2phi); near phi = 0 and pi the bracket is 4, giving shifts of 2M/b.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 3 writes sqrt(-g_00) ~ 1 + 2 Phi; the weak-field result is -g_00 ~ 1 + 2 Phi, so the square root is about 1 + Phi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Factor-of-two confusion about how strongly clocks and coordinate light speed depend on the potential.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State g_00 ~ -(1 + 2 Phi) and derive sqrt(-g_00) ~ 1 + Phi explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text calls sqrt(-g_00) a refractive index; since n = c/c', with flat spatial metric the index is 1/sqrt(-g_00), and g_00 alone yields only half the deflection.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may build an optics model that bends light the wrong way or gives Soldner's value.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the isotropic weak-field index n ~ 1 - 2 Phi, which includes the spatial metric and reproduces 4M/b.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Summary table entry for massive dr/dtau has L-tilde/r^2 instead of L-tilde^2/r^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Copying the table into a numerical integrator gives wrong orbits.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use (1 - 2M/r)(1 + L^2/r^2), consistent with the dr/dt row just below.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Delta phi means the total swept angle in Fig. 24.3 but the deflection in the text and eqn 24.23.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers comparing figure and text may think the deflection is pi + 4M/b or vice versa.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Reserve delta for the deflection 4M/b and Delta for the swept angle pi + 4M/b.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The critical-angle discussion does not mention that sin psi = s has two solutions; for r > 3M the relevant psi_c is obtuse and the captured cone surrounds the inward direction, for r < 3M it is acute. Capture also depends on whether the ray is initially inward or outward.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners taking arcsin naively conclude that most outward photons fall in, or cannot reconcile 'critical angle becomes smaller' with the formula.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Tabulate psi_c against r (152 deg at 10M, 135 deg at 6M, 90 deg at 3M, 45 deg near 2.2M) and draw the escape cone explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The remark that b decreases with increasing energy because energetic particles scatter less imports massive-particle intuition; for light b is purely geometric.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Invites the false belief that deflection is frequency dependent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize that L and E scale together for a photon and that 4M/b is achromatic, a consequence of the equivalence principle.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text describes sin psi as a sideways part of the photon's coordinate velocity, yet eqn 24.33 is built from orthonormal-frame (locally measured) components.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs the coordinate versus measured distinction that the section depends on.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'sideways velocity measured by the static observer'.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 24.4's rubber sheet and caption attribute the bending to curved space; the split into time and space contributions is not discussed in this chapter.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces a popular picture that yields only half the effect.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show that keeping only g_tt gives 2M/b and adding g_rr gives the other 2M/b; link to Chapter 23's note that rubber sheets omit time curvature.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Cross-chapter inconsistency: Chapter 6 says its equivalence-principle estimate is a third of the true bending, while this chapter says GR is about twice the Newtonian value; the standard decomposition is half from g_tt and half from spatial curvature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers who remember Chapter 6 may be confused about which factor is right.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Tutor should state the factor-of-two relation clearly and treat the Chapter 6 heuristic as order-of-magnitude only.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The capture discussion speaks of photons being destroyed at r = 0 and of the critical angle vanishing at r = 2M, without noting that no static observer can exist at or inside 2M and that the horizon is the real point of no return.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misleading picture of what happens at 2M and of what 'destroyed' means.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Restrict the emitter formula to r > 2M and preview Chapter 25's horizon discussion.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Perturbative solution silently drops the homogeneous solution and the approximation 3u^2 ~ 3u0^2 is described only briefly; accuracy limits (M/b small) are not quantified.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Unclear why the answer is unique and when 4M/b fails (strong deflection near b = sqrt(27) M, where deflection diverges).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show that a homogeneous term just redefines b and orientation, and plot exact versus first-order deflection as b approaches the critical value.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Gravitational lensing, magnification, multiple images and the Einstein angle are relegated to one example and one exercise; the book (published before recent imaging) gives no observational lensing numbers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The connection to one of the most used GR tools in astronomy is thin.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add worked numbers for microlensing (milliarcsecond rings) and galaxy lenses (arcsecond rings), and a simulated sky.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 24.7 labels the dotted level touching the peak as 1/b^2 while drawing the capture arrow above it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Ambiguity whether the arrow's energy or the dotted line is the photon's 1/b^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the peak height 1/(27M^2) and put 1/b^2 on the arrow.

tutor_notes: Open with a prediction question: 'Light has no mass. Should the Sun bend it at all, and if so would you expect GR to give more or less than Newton?' Record the guess and return to it after Example 24.5.
Before new algebra, ask the learner to recall the massive-particle energy equation and V_eff from Chapter 23; then have them predict what changes when u.u = -1 becomes 0.

Order of explanation: null condition -> effective energy equation -> read W_eff plot (peak, no well) -> impact parameter meaning -> orbit equation -> perturbative deflection -> numbers -> lensing -> what an observer sees.
Stress early that only b matters for a photon's path, so deflection is independent of colour; use this to defuse the text's energy-scattering remark.
Check for understanding: 'Why can't light orbit stably around a black hole?' (no minimum of W_eff) and 'What happens to a ray with b slightly less than sqrt(27) M?' (winds near 3M, then plunges).

When deriving the deflection, have the learner find where u = 0 on the straight line first (phi = 0 and pi), then ask how a small positive correction shifts those zeros; point out the typo in printed eqn 24.22.
Give concrete scales: M_sun is about 1.5 km, the solar limb is 7e5 km, so M/b ~ 2e-6 and the deflection is 8.5e-6 rad, about 1.75 arcsec; Newton gives half.
If the learner likes optics, use the refractive-index picture but correct it: the index is about 1 - 2 Phi including space curvature; g_tt alone gives the Newtonian half.
Common question: 'Does light slow down near the Sun?' Answer: coordinate speed changes (this is also the Shapiro delay of Chapter 8), local speed is always c.
For Section 24.2, make the learner say out loud which components are coordinate and which are measured; then sanity-check sin psi = b/r far from the mass.
Walk through the critical angle at a few radii (10M, 6M, 3M, 2.5M) and explicitly handle the obtuse versus acute branch; the half-sky result at 3M is memorable.

Close by reversing time to predict the dark region on the sky, and ask how large it looks from far away (about sqrt(27) M/D, bigger than the 2M horizon radius); bridge to the Event Horizon Telescope image in Chapter 25.
Common question: 'Is the Einstein ring real?' Yes; galaxy lenses give arcsecond rings, stars in our Galaxy give milliarcsecond rings detected as brightenings.
For advanced learners, suggest numerically integrating u'' + u = 3u^2 to see the deflection grow without bound as b approaches sqrt(27) M.
